# Exercise 5.2 — Classification metrics {#sec-classification-metrics}

**45 minutes · individually**

:::: {.web-only}
Every cell on this page is a real R or Python cell, run against
`data/diabetes.csv`. Open `day5-02-classification-metrics.qmd` in your editor
and run them one at a time.
::::

## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Compute accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC from predicted
  probabilities, in both languages, and say which rows each one looked at.
- State the accuracy of the majority-class rule for a dataset before you fit
  anything, and report every later accuracy next to it.
- Explain how a model can be a percentage point better than that rule, find
  one diabetic patient in eight, and still have an AUC well above chance.
:::

## Why this, here

@sec-regression-metrics ended where the outcome stops being a number. The
outcome here is `pos` or `neg`, so the residual is no longer a distance and
every metric on this page is built instead from counts in a 2×2 table. The
table has two error types, the two are not interchangeable in a clinic, and
accuracy — the metric everybody reaches for first — adds them together with
weights chosen by the prevalence of the disease rather than by anyone's
judgement.

The data is the synthetic diabetes extract described in @sec-data-diabetes; the
split is 70/30 and stratified, which is what @sec-leakage argued for.

## Worked example — fit, and look at the table before the metrics

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(tidymodels); library(readr)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv") |>
  dplyr::mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("pos", "neg")))

table(diabetes$diabetes)

set.seed(123)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.7, strata = diabetes)
train <- training(split); test <- testing(split)

age_fit <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") |> fit(diabetes ~ age, data = train)

test_preds <- augment(age_fit, test)
conf_mat(test_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)
```

## Python

```{python}
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, recall_score, roc_auc_score,
                             confusion_matrix, roc_curve)

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
y = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
print(diabetes["diabetes"].value_counts())

X_age = diabetes[["age"]]
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X_age, y, test_size=0.3,
                                          random_state=123, stratify=y)

age_fit = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
confusion_matrix(y_te, age_fit.predict(X_te), labels=[1, 0])
```
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Which class is the event is a decision, and the two languages ask for it differently
In R, yardstick treats the **first level of the factor** as the event, so
`factor(diabetes, levels = c("pos", "neg"))` is load-bearing: drop it, `neg`
becomes the event, and your sensitivity and specificity silently swap places.
In Python the convention is that the event is coded `1`, which is why the
outcome is converted with `== "pos"` and why `labels=[1, 0]` is passed to
`confusion_matrix` to get the same orientation as R's.

Nothing warns you if you get this wrong. The symptom is a model that looks
implausibly good at ruling out a common disease.
:::

Now the metrics, on the rows the model was fitted to and on the held-out rows.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
class_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, sens, yardstick::specificity, precision)

dplyr::bind_rows(
  class_metrics(augment(age_fit, train), truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class) |>
    dplyr::mutate(set = "train"),
  class_metrics(test_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class) |>
    dplyr::mutate(set = "test")
) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = .metric, names_from = set, values_from = .estimate)
```

## Python

```{python}
def scores(model, X, yy):
    pred = model.predict(X)
    return {"accuracy": accuracy_score(yy, pred),
            "sens":     recall_score(yy, pred),
            "spec":     recall_score(1 - yy, 1 - pred),
            "auc":      roc_auc_score(yy, model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1])}

pd.DataFrame({"train": scores(age_fit, X_tr, y_tr),
              "test":  scores(age_fit, X_te, y_te)})
```
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## `spec` is not `specificity`
In R, writing `spec` inside `metric_set()` picks up `readr::spec`, the function
that reports a column specification, and `metric_set()` fails with a message
about mixing metric types. Write `yardstick::specificity`. This is the most
common five-minute delay on this page.
:::

## Worked example — the ROC curve, which does not need a threshold

Everything above was computed after turning probabilities into classes at 0.5.
That threshold is a separate decision from the model (@sec-thresholds). An ROC
curve shows what the model can do at *every* threshold at once: each point is
one threshold, plotting sensitivity against 1 − specificity.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 4.2
roc_curve(test_preds, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos) |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(title = "Age-only logistic model, test set")

roc_auc(test_preds, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 4.2
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_te, age_fit.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.2, 3.6))
ax.plot(fpr, tpr)
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", color="grey")
ax.set_xlabel("1 - specificity"); ax.set_ylabel("sensitivity")
ax.set_title("Age-only logistic model, test set")
plt.show()

roc_auc_score(y_te, age_fit.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1])
```
:::

The AUC is the area under that curve. It has one honest interpretation worth
memorising: **take one patient with diabetes and one without, at random; the
AUC is the probability the model gives the diabetic patient the higher score.**
It is a statement about ranking, it never looks at the threshold, and 0.5 is
the value you get by ranking at random.

## Task 1 — The bar every accuracy has to clear

Before comparing models, compute the accuracy of the rule *predict `neg` for
everybody*. It uses no predictors, needs no fitting, and is the number your
accuracy has to beat before it means anything.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
majority_accuracy <- mean(test$diabetes == ______)
majority_accuracy

model_accuracy <- accuracy(test_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)$.estimate
check_beats_prevalence(model_accuracy, ______)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank is a class label in quotation marks — the commoner of the two.
The second is the vector of true outcomes for the rows the accuracy was
computed on; the check works out the majority share itself.

```{r}
majority_accuracy <- mean(test$diabetes == "neg")
majority_accuracy

model_accuracy <- accuracy(test_preds, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)$.estimate

```

## Task 2 — Earn the AUC: use every predictor

Fit a second logistic model with all eight predictors, on the same training
rows, and report accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC on the same test
rows.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
full_fit <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") |> fit(______, data = train)

full_test <- augment(full_fit, test)
class_metrics(full_test, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)
roc_auc(full_test, truth = diabetes, ______)

check_metric_range(roc_auc(full_test, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos)$.estimate,
                   0.7, 0.95, "test AUC, all predictors")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
A formula with every other column on the right-hand side has a one-character
shorthand in R. The second blank is the column holding the probability of the
event, which `augment()` has already added.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
full_fit <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") |> fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

full_test <- augment(full_fit, test)
class_metrics(full_test, truth = diabetes, estimate = .pred_class)
roc_auc(full_test, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos)

check_metric_range(roc_auc(full_test, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos)$.estimate,
                   0.7, 0.95, "test AUC, all predictors")
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false

print(scores(full_fit, Xf_te, y_te))
check_metric_range(roc_auc_score(y_te, full_fit.predict_proba(Xf_te)[:, 1]),
```

```{python}
X_full = diabetes.drop(columns="diabetes")
Xf_tr, Xf_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X_full, y, test_size=0.3,
                                            random_state=123, stratify=y)
full_fit = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)).fit(Xf_tr, y_tr)

print(scores(full_fit, Xf_te, y_te))
check_metric_range(roc_auc_score(y_te, full_fit.predict_proba(Xf_te)[:, 1]),
```

Which of the four numbers improved most, in percentage points? It is not
accuracy, and the reason is the subject of the next section.

## Task 3 — A control: break the model on purpose

An AUC of 0.68 from one predictor is either a weak signal or no signal reported
confidently. The way to tell is to destroy the signal and see what the
machinery reports. Shuffle the **training** outcomes so that no predictor can
carry information about them, refit the full model, and score it on the
untouched test rows. Do it ten times, because one shuffle tells you nothing.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
shuffled_auc <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  train_shuf <- train |> dplyr::mutate(diabetes = ______(diabetes))
  f <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") |> fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train_shuf)
  roc_auc(augment(f, test), truth = diabetes, .pred_pos)$.estimate
}
aucs <- vapply(1:10, shuffled_auc, numeric(1))
round(range(aucs), 3)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Shuffling a vector is sampling it without replacement, in full. One base R
function does exactly that and takes no other argument.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
shuffled_auc <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  train_shuf <- train |> dplyr::mutate(diabetes = sample(diabetes))
  f <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") |> fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train_shuf)
  roc_auc(augment(f, test), truth = diabetes, .pred_pos)$.estimate
}
aucs <- vapply(1:10, shuffled_auc, numeric(1))
round(range(aucs), 3)
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
aucs = []
for _ in range(10):
    y_shuf = rng.______(y_tr.to_numpy())
    f = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)).fit(Xf_tr, y_shuf)
    aucs.append(roc_auc_score(y_te, f.predict_proba(Xf_te)[:, 1]))
round(min(aucs), 3), round(max(aucs), 3)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
aucs = []
for _ in range(10):
    y_shuf = rng.permutation(y_tr.to_numpy())
    f = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)).fit(Xf_tr, y_shuf)
    aucs.append(roc_auc_score(y_te, f.predict_proba(Xf_te)[:, 1]))
round(min(aucs), 3), round(max(aucs), 3)
```
:::
:::
:::

The shuffled AUCs do not sit on 0.5. Ours spanned roughly 0.28 to 0.74 across
the two languages. That spread is the width of an AUC estimated on 231
patients when there is nothing to estimate, and it is the yardstick against
which the age-only model's 0.66–0.70 should be read.

## The result that should bother you

On the held-out rows, the age-only model's accuracy is about 0.63–0.65. The
rule "predict `neg` for everybody" scores 0.636. In R's split the model is
1.7 percentage points above that rule; in Python's split it is 0.9 points
below it. And the model's sensitivity is around 0.11–0.12: of the 84
test patients who have diabetes, it identifies nine or ten.

Three steps.

1. Accuracy is a weighted average of sensitivity and specificity, with the
   weights fixed by prevalence — here 36% and 64%. A model can raise its
   accuracy by abandoning the minority class entirely, and at a threshold of
   0.5 a weak model does exactly that: it predicts `neg` for almost everyone,
   inherits the majority rule's accuracy, and loses almost nothing.
2. So an accuracy near the prevalence of the commonest class is not evidence of
   a working model. It is the signature of a model that has declined to make a
   decision. Always print the majority-class accuracy first; it costs one line
   and it is the only context in which the second line can be read.
3. Yet the same model's AUC is around 0.66–0.70, which is not nothing. AUC
   ignores the threshold and asks only whether diabetic patients are ranked
   above non-diabetic ones. There is a real but weak ordering in `age`;
   accuracy at 0.5 threw it away. Two metrics, same model, two conclusions —
   and both are correct answers to different questions.

The full model, by contrast, reaches a test AUC of about 0.78–0.84 and a
sensitivity of 0.49–0.57. It is the sensitivity that moved, from one patient in
eight to about one in two, and sensitivity is the number a screening programme
would be commissioned on.

## Reflection

1. A paper reports 94% accuracy for a model detecting a condition with a
   prevalence of 5%. Write the one sentence you would put in your review.
2. AUC does not change when you change the threshold, and accuracy does. Give a
   clinical situation where that makes AUC the right summary, and one where it
   makes AUC the wrong one.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Expected values** (the two languages split differently; both are given, and
regenerated data moves the last digit).

| | R, seed 123 | Python, random_state 123 |
|---|---|---|
| class counts | 280 `pos`, 488 `neg` | same |
| majority-class accuracy, test | 0.636 | 0.636 |
| age-only, train acc / sens / spec | 0.618 / 0.128 / 0.900 | 0.628 / 0.148 / 0.903 |
| age-only, test acc / sens / spec | 0.654 / 0.119 / 0.959 | 0.628 / 0.107 / 0.925 |
| age-only, test AUC | 0.678 | 0.699 |
| all predictors, test acc / sens / spec | 0.758 / 0.488 / 0.912 | 0.740 / 0.571 / 0.837 |
| all predictors, test AUC | 0.844 | 0.782 |
| shuffled-outcome test AUC, 10 runs | 0.28 to 0.66 | 0.34 to 0.74 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[40,30,30]"}

**The sign flip is useful, not a defect.** In R the age-only model passes
`check_beats_prevalence` by 1.7 points and in Python it fails it by 0.9. Put
both on the board. A difference that changes whether the model "beats
baseline" but is entirely produced by which rows landed in the test set is the
cleanest argument for resampling that the week provides, and it sets up
@sec-decision-trees, where every tuning decision rests on a resampled estimate.

**Watch for.** (1) Omitting the `levels = c("pos", "neg")` relevel in R:
sensitivity and specificity swap, and the model appears to have a sensitivity
of 0.96. Ask anyone reporting a sensitivity above 0.9 to print
`levels(train$diabetes)`. (2) `spec` versus `yardstick::specificity`. (3)
Reading `recall_score(1 - y, 1 - pred)` as a trick — it is the definition of
specificity, and it is worth saying that out loud.

**Timing.** Task 3 takes five minutes and is the task to protect. If you must
cut, cut the ROC plot in one language.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — Make accuracy look excellent
Keep every `neg` patient and a random 10% of the `pos` patients, re-split, and
refit the age-only model. Report accuracy. Then report sensitivity. You have
changed nothing about the model or the predictors.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — AUC is not everything either
Two models can share an AUC of 0.80 and disagree completely about which
patients are highest risk. Fit the all-predictor model and a model using only
`glucose`, compare their AUCs, then compare the ranks they assign to the twenty
highest-risk test patients. Which of the two would you rather hand to a triage
nurse?
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 3 — Balanced accuracy
Compute `(sensitivity + specificity) / 2` for both models. What does it score
for the majority-class rule, and why is that the property that makes it worth
reporting?
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can evaluate a classifier honestly — against the
majority-class rule, with both error types shown separately, and with AUC
reported as a property of the ranking rather than of any decision.

**Cannot:** that the model you evaluated is the best one available, or that
either of today's models is flexible enough for this data. A logistic
regression can only draw one straight boundary. @sec-decision-trees fits a
model that can draw as many as it likes, which turns out to be the problem.
